title: Phase-sensitive mean values and pretentious distance
pvg_object: unit-modulus or bounded weights attached to labeled prime coordinates, including character and logarithmic phases
ant_object: Halasz mean-value theory and pretentious distance to chi(n)n^{it}
forward_translation: Encode prime-coordinate phase alignment through the distance sum_p<=x (1-Re(f(p) conjugate(g(p))))/p and route mean values by proximity to structured models.
reverse_translation: A large or small mean constrains possible pretentious models but does not uniquely recover all prime phases.
preserved_information: aggregate phase alignment with candidate characters and Archimedean twists
lost_information: individual prime phases and local exceptional behavior
trigger: A bounded multiplicative function has cancellation or bias not explained by additive probabilistic cards.
typical_output: a structured obstruction chi(n)n^{it}, a distance lower bound, or a mean-value estimate
error_or_wall: Support-only geometry erases the phase correlations that govern multiplicative cancellation.
required_certificate: Define the comparison class, estimate the pretentious distance uniformly, and match the quantitative Halasz theorem used.
positive_example: A Dirichlet character has zero pretentious distance to itself on primes away from its conductor.
counterexample: Bounded multiplicativity alone does not distinguish random-looking cancellation from hidden character correlation.
anti_overclaim: Small empirical mean is not a certificate of nonpretentiousness.
classification: Phase-sensitive analytic route / no additive-model substitution
source_basis: Halasz mean-value theory and pretentious multiplicative functions

title: Kubilius model and transfer from local coordinates to integers
pvg_object: a product model for prime-coordinate valuations with approximately geometric marginals
ant_object: Kubilius-type approximation and probabilistic number-theory transfer to integers n<=x
forward_translation: Local independent variables may model selected valuations only after truncating primes and quantifying total-variation, moment, or characteristic-function error under the size constraint.
reverse_translation: An integer limiting law supports a model for chosen observables but does not prove literal independence of all valuation coordinates.
preserved_information: specified low-dimensional marginals and observables within the certified range
lost_information: global product constraint, large-prime dependence, and boundary effects near x
trigger: Independent prime-coordinate variables are used to predict a distribution on integers.
typical_output: a quantitative comparison theorem and an admissible prime truncation
error_or_wall: The condition n<=x couples coordinates and invalidates unrestricted independence.
required_certificate: State the modeled coordinates, truncation range, comparison metric, and uniform approximation error.
positive_example: For fixed small primes, P(p|n)=floor(x/p)/x=1/p+O(1/x), but joint transfer needs a theorem.
counterexample: Independent geometric variables can assign positive mass to products exceeding x.
anti_overclaim: The Kubilius model is an approximation, not an identity of probability spaces.
source_basis: Classical probabilistic number theory and Kubilius models

title: Short intervals and additive-order localization
pvg_object: a thin logarithmic valuation slab together with information absent from multiplicative coordinates about consecutive integer order
ant_object: mean values and limiting laws in intervals [x,x+h]
forward_translation: A global valuation statistic must be supplemented by a short-interval theorem controlling additive localization, endpoint dependence, and the permitted range of h.
reverse_translation: A short-interval law gives localized information for the observable but still does not make neighboring integers geometrically close in valuation space.
preserved_information: the observable's distribution within the certified interval length range
lost_information: individual integer order and transfer outside that h range
trigger: A global average or Erdos--Kac law is asserted in intervals shorter than x.
typical_output: an explicit lower range for h and a uniform local error
error_or_wall: Multiplicative valuation geometry does not encode successor order; global laws can fail or require new input locally.
required_certificate: Prove uniformity in the interval base point and length, including exceptional intervals and endpoint errors.
positive_example: Global density one-half for even integers does not determine every interval of length one.
counterexample: A global normal law supplies no theorem for h=x^theta without localized estimates.
anti_overclaim: A logarithmic slab is not an additive neighborhood certificate.
